why use exceptions? right off the bat, how do you signal an error in a constructor? you have no return type to do it with. are you going to have some kind of member boolean that signals whether or not the object is properly constructed, and then call a function to verify after every construction? that would be ugly as fuck and would be very prone to misuse(if you forgot and instantiated it without checking or you were working with other programmers) exceptions are perfect for this.

the issue of having to verify each time the error code with an if statement isn't just for my constructor example. look at the disgusting FAILED macro and NTSTATUS garbage windows uses. are you going to create an enum for every function that can fail in multiple ways? and then upon each call site, start branching on the result to handle the error properly? also, you've now given up your return value and now you've got to use some ugly references or the like in order to get values out of the function.

with exceptions you throw whenever and whatever you want, and worry about it later. the call site doesn't have to worry about it either. in the function that calls it, after the body you have all your error processing code neatly organized by which type to catch. oh, and you don't have to handle it there either. you can just not and pass the buck to the next function down the call stack. you don't have to give up your return value. it works with constructors. you don't have to make any enums. also exceptions enforce error handling, where if you forget to handle errors in a typical error code scheme you probably won't find out.
